context_description: One of the most essential Korean words. Used to express deep affection between lovers, family members, and close friends. It appears frequently in K-dramas and K-pop songs.
The most polite and universally safe way to say thank you in Korean. Use this with strangers, elders, or in any formal situation.
The standard greeting in Korean, appropriate for almost all situations. Literally means 'Are you at peace?' and is used any time of day.
Said to someone who is leaving while you stay. If you are the one leaving, say '안녕히 계세요' instead. This distinction is unique to Korean.
The most formal and polite way to apologize in Korean. Use this when you bump into someone, make a mistake at work, or need to show sincere regret.
example_sentence_english: I am sorry for being late.

context_description: The standard polite way to say yes. In casual speech, Koreans often say '응 (Eung)' instead. '네' is safe to use in all situations.
The polite way to say no in Korean. In casual conversation, '아니 (Ani)' is used. Koreans sometimes avoid saying no directly to be polite.
An essential word for food lovers visiting Korea. Use '맛있어요' (polite) when complimenting someone's cooking. Koreans love hearing foreigners use this word!
A survival word in Korea. At restaurants, water is usually free and self-service. Saying '물 주세요' will get you water anywhere.
example_sentence_english: Please give me a glass of water.

context_description: In Korean culture, '친구' specifically refers to someone the same age as you. People older or younger are called '형/누나/오빠/언니' or '동생' instead.
Family is central to Korean culture. Korean has very specific terms for each family member depending on whether you are male or female.
Used to describe scenery, art, or deep beauty. For calling someone pretty in casual conversation, Koreans more commonly use '예쁘다 (yeppeuda)'.
example_sentence_english: Autumn in Korea is truly beautiful.

context_description: Koreans use this word constantly — for babies, pets, accessories, and even food. '귀여워!' is one of the most frequently heard exclamations in daily Korean life.
Expresses a deep sense of happiness or contentment. For everyday cheerfulness, Koreans often use '기쁘다 (gippeuda)' or '좋다 (jota)' instead.
example_sentence_english: I am happy because I am with you.

context_description: Used to express sadness or sorrow. You will hear this word a lot in Korean ballads and dramas. The adjective form '슬픈 (seulpeun)' is also very common.
Literally means 'fire rises.' The expression '화가 나다' is used when you feel anger building up. In slang, Koreans say '빡치다' but this is very informal.
Literally means 'stomach is empty.' Food culture is huge in Korea, so this phrase comes in handy multiple times a day. Often used to suggest eating together.
example_sentence_english: I'm hungry. Shall we go eat?

context_description: One of the most relatable words in Korean work culture. Korea has a demanding work-life balance, so you will hear and use this word very often.
Korea has one of the highest coffee consumption rates in the world. The word is borrowed from English. '아메리카노 (Americano)' is by far the most popular order.
example_sentence_english: Would you like to have a cup of coffee?

context_description: In Korean, '밥' means both rice and meal. '밥 먹었어?' (Have you eaten rice?) is a common way to greet someone and show you care about them.
example_sentence_english: Have you eaten? (Literally: Have you had rice?)

context_description: Education is extremely valued in Korean society. Students often attend school from early morning until late at night including private academies called '학원 (hagwon)'.
example_sentence_english: What time do you go to school?

context_description: Teachers are highly respected in Korean culture. The suffix '님' adds honor. This title is also used for doctors, lawyers, and other respected professionals.
Used broadly for anyone who studies. Shop owners and taxi drivers often call young people '학생' even if they are not sure of their status.
example_sentence_english: I am a student learning Korean.

context_description: Korea has a rich literary tradition and reading culture. '책방 (chaekbang)' means bookstore, and '도서관 (doseogwan)' means library.
Korea has excellent and affordable healthcare. Even small clinics are called '병원'. For emergencies, '응급실 (eunggeupsil)' means emergency room.
example_sentence_english: I need to go to the hospital.

context_description: Korean currency is the Won (원). Prices in Korea can seem high in numbers (a coffee might be 5,000 won) but are reasonable in value.
example_sentence_english: How much is this? (I don't have enough money.)

context_description: Korea has four distinct seasons. Talking about weather is a common conversation starter, just like in English. Summers are hot and humid, winters are cold and dry.
example_sentence_english: The weather is really nice today.

context_description: Korea has an excellent rail system. KTX is the high-speed train connecting Seoul to Busan in about 2.5 hours. The subway is called '지하철 (jihacheol)'.
example_sentence_english: I will go to Busan by train.

context_description: Incheon International Airport is consistently ranked among the best in the world. '인천공항 (Incheon Gonghang)' is the main international gateway to Korea.
example_sentence_english: How long does it take to get to the airport?

context_description: A loanword from English pronounced with Korean phonetics. Budget travelers often stay at '게스트하우스 (guesthouse)' or '모텔 (motel)' which are much cheaper.
Literally means 'makeup room.' This is a must-know survival word. Public restrooms in Korea are generally very clean and well-maintained.
Used when you need to get someone's attention politely or when passing through a crowd. In restaurants, Koreans call staff by saying '저기요 (jeogiyo)' instead.
example_sentence_english: Excuse me, may I ask for directions?

context_description: Essential for shopping and eating out in Korea. '이거 얼마예요?' is the complete phrase. In traditional markets, you can often negotiate the price.
Useful when bargaining at Korean traditional markets like Namdaemun or Dongdaemun. The opposite is '비싸다 (bissada)' meaning expensive.
Housing and beef are notoriously expensive in Korea. If something is too pricey, you can say '너무 비싸요' to express that the price is too high.
example_sentence_english: Housing prices in Seoul are too expensive.

context_description: A very useful phrase when you are lost or confused. Adding '잘' before it ('잘 모르겠어요') softens the expression and sounds more natural.
Also used as the 'Like' button on Korean social media. '좋아요' can mean both 'It's good' and 'I like it' depending on context. Very versatile word.
Expresses dislike or refusal. Can sound strong, so Koreans often soften it by saying '별로예요 (byeolloieyo)' meaning 'not really' or 'it's not great.'
Attached to the end of a request. Literally means 'please give me.' For example, '물 주세요' means 'Water, please.' One of the most useful patterns in Korean.
Means 'just a moment please.' Very commonly used in daily life — at restaurants, stores, or when someone is talking too fast. Often shortened to '잠깐!'
example_sentence_english: Wait a moment, I'll be there soon!

context_description: Used for birthdays, weddings, promotions, and achievements. '생일 축하합니다' is the Korean version of 'Happy Birthday.'
Can mean both 'work' and 'matter/thing.' Korea is known for its strong work ethic. '회사 (hoesa)' means company, and '직장 (jikjang)' means workplace.
example_sentence_english: I have a lot of work today.

context_description: K-pop has made Korean music world-famous. '노래 (norae)' means song, and '노래방 (noraebang)' is the Korean word for karaoke room — a must-do activity in Korea.
example_sentence_english: I often listen to Korean music.

context_description: Korean cinema is world-renowned, with films like Parasite winning the Academy Award. '영화관 (yeonghwagwan)' means movie theater.
example_sentence_english: Shall we watch a movie this weekend?

context_description: Literally means 'electric talk.' Mobile phone is '핸드폰 (haendeupon)' or '휴대폰 (hyudaepon).' Korea has some of the fastest mobile networks in the world.
An important emergency phrase. '도와주세요' is polite and urgent. In a real emergency, you can shout '살려주세요 (sallyeojuseyo)' which means 'Save me!'
Korean uses two number systems for telling time — native Korean numbers for hours and Sino-Korean numbers for minutes. '몇 시예요?' means 'What time is it?'
Literally means 'male friend.' Often shortened to '남친 (namchin)' in casual speech. Korean dating culture has unique terms like '썸 (sseom)' for the flirting stage.
Literally means 'female friend.' Often shortened to '여친 (yeochin).' In Korea, couples celebrate monthly anniversaries and have matching couple items.
Used when toasting drinks. Korean drinking culture has many rules — always pour for elders with two hands and turn your head away when drinking in front of them.
